parent.name: Bishop's Opening: Berlin Defense
parent.overview: White's bishop on c4 eyes f7 and Black answers with 2...Nf6, hitting e4 at once. White's standard reply is 3.d3 (defending e4 and keeping f4 and later c3/d4 available); 3.Nc3 transposes to a Vienna Game and 3.Nf3 to the Italian or Two Knights. Black usually continues 3...c6 (Paulsen) planning ...d5 to hit the bishop with tempo, or 3...Nc6/...Bc5 reaching the quiet Giuoco Pianissimo. Most play is therefore a calm Italian-style game with a small White space edge. Sharper options exist but are rare: 3.d4 (Urusov Gambit, a pawn for attack) and 3.f4 (Greco Gambit, transposing to the Bishop's Gambit after ...exf4). Nick de Firmian's verdict is that the Berlin leads to equality with best play.

parent.name: English Opening: Anglo-Indian Defense
parent.overview: 1.c4 Nf6 is a crossroads, not a single structure. Black develops a piece, covers e4 and d5, and waits to see whether White wants d4 (which usually transposes into the King's Indian, Nimzo-Indian, Queen's Indian or Grünfeld) or a pure English set-up. The main branches are 2.Nc3 (with ...e6 giving Nimzo or Hedgehog-type play, ...g6 a King's Indian set-up, ...d5 a reversed Grünfeld, ...c5 or ...e5 symmetrical or reversed-Sicilian structures), 2.g3 and 2.Nf3. The typical English middlegame is a manoeuvring game with White's pressure on d5 and queenside space against Black's central break (...d5 or ...e5), but 2.Nc3 e6 3.e4 (Mikėnas-Carls) can be sharper. Black's choice of branch decides almost everything about character and structure.

root.name: Sicilian Defense: Franco-Sicilian Variation
root.moves: 1. e4 c5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. d4 e6

parent.name: Sicilian Defense: Open
parent.overview: After 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 Black has developed the knight to c6 before choosing a set-up, so the root is a crossroads: Classical (5.Nc3 d6), Sveshnikov (5...e5 after ...Nf6), Four Knights (5...e6), Kalashnikov or Lowenthal (4...e5), Accelerated Dragon (4...g6) and Taimanov-type lines (s1, s2, s3). White gets a development lead and kingside space, Black gets the open c-file and a central pawn majority, so the play is unbalanced and complex (s1). The Richter-Rauzer (6.Bg5) and Sozin (6.Bc4) lead to a race where White attacks on the kingside, often castling queenside, and Black counters with ...a6, ...b5 and c-file pressure (s2). Statistics are balanced (White 47.7%, Black 47.3% in 5.6 million Lichess games, per the Chessiverse page for the Four Knights) (s3).

parent.name: Queen's Gambit Accepted
parent.moves: 1. d4 d5 2. c4 dxc4 3. Nf3 Nf6
parent.overview: After 2...dxc4 Black has taken the c-pawn, but sources agree he cannot keep it without serious concessions; White regains it with Bxc4 once the e-pawn has moved (3.e3 or 3.Nf3 then e3, or 3.e4). Black instead gives up the idea of holding it and fights for central counterplay: ...c5 (and ...cxd4) or ...e5 to undermine d4, and ...a6 with ...b5 to gain queenside space and time for the c8 bishop. The centre is open, White has the d4/e4 pawns and the move, and the usual middlegames are IQP or hanging-pawn positions with piece play. Character varies by line: the 3.Nf3 Nf6 4.e3 e6 5.Bxc4 c5 main line is positional and balanced, while 3.e4 lines can be tactical early. It is sound and has been a regular at the elite level since the 1990s.

root.name: Italian Game: Rousseau Gambit
root.moves: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 f5

parent.name: Italian Game
parent.overview: White develops the bishop to c4 aiming at f7 and prepares to take the centre with c3 and d4 or, more quietly, d3 (s1, s2). The root is a crossroads: 3...Bc5 (Giuoco Piano) mirrors White's set-up, 3...Nf6 (Two Knights) invites sharper play, and 3...Be7 (Hungarian) is passive and solid (own understanding for the last). Today's main practical line is the Giuoco Pianissimo with c3, d3 and slow manoeuvring, which became fashionable in the 1980s-2000s and again in the 21st century as a way to avoid the Berlin (s1). The older 4.c3 and d4 lines and the Evans Gambit are sharper (s1). It is fundamentally sound with modest winning chances (s1). It is described as accessible to beginners yet used by Giri, So and Vachier-Lagrave (s3).
